- Colostomy, ileostomy, and urostomy each shape output and daily care a little differently `1.1`
- A stoma can be temporary or permanent — your care team decides with you `1.2`
- Healthy peristomal skin should look like the skin on the other side of your abdomen `1.3`

### 02 · The less common diversions
Group: **Start here** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

**Other stomas you may hear about** `2.s1`

- Jejunostomy — formed higher in the small bowel than an ileostomy. Output is greater and more watery, and fluid, salt and nutrition need closer specialist follow-up `2.s1.1`
- Ileal conduit — the most common form of urostomy, where urine is diverted through a short piece of bowel to a stoma `2.s1.2`
- Nephrostomy — a tube that drains urine straight from the kidney. It comes out through the skin of your back rather than through a stoma on the abdomen, and drains into a bag usually strapped to your thigh under your clothes. It is often temporary `2.s1.3`

**Continent diversions, which work differently** `2.s2`

- An ileoanal pouch (often called a J-pouch) is designed to leave you with no stoma in the long run — an internal reservoir is joined to the anus, so you pass stool the usual way. It normally takes two or three operations, and most people have a temporary ileostomy for a few months in between. Once it is working, stool is looser and you go more often, commonly five to ten times a day, settling with time `2.s2.1`
- A continent ileostomy, such as a Kock pouch, has a small flush stoma and an internal reservoir made from small bowel. There is no pouch to wear — you drain it with a catheter, usually two to four times a day, and cover the stoma with a cap or gauze in between `2.s2.2`
- A Mitrofanoff is a different operation, for urine rather than stool. A narrow channel, usually made from the appendix, runs from your own bladder to a small stoma, and you pass a catheter through it to empty `2.s2.3`

> **Note** `2.s2.note` — Continent diversions are cared for quite differently from a conventional stoma. Advice about pouches, barriers and flanges will not apply to you — advice about diet, fluids and salt still does. Two things this site does not cover. With a bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch, if the catheter will not pass, stop rather than persisting, rest an hour and try again, and get advice that day if you still cannot drain. With a Mitrofanoff, which drains urine, do not keep trying — an unemptied bladder needs an emergency department the same day. Your surgical team and NSWOC are the right source for both.

> **Note** `2.note` — NSWOCC publishes free patient guides for several of these, including jejunostomy and gastrostomy, in English and French. They are linked from Everyday Liivving.

### 03 · Words you will hear
Group: **Start here** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

**Your equipment** `3.s1`

- Appliance or pouching system — the whole setup: the barrier plus the pouch `3.s1.1`
- Barrier, wafer or baseplate — the part that sticks to your skin. Many people say flange for this too, but on some two-piece systems flange means the plastic ring that clicks the pouch on. If you are ordering, check which one your brand means `3.s1.2`
- Convexity — a barrier that curves outward towards your skin instead of lying flat, to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out or to smooth a crease. It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths. Helpful for some abdomens, harmful for others, so it is an assessment rather than a purchase `3.s1.3`

**Your body** `3.s2`

- Peristomal skin — the skin around the stoma. It starts where the stoma meets your skin and takes in everything your barrier, tape or belt touches `3.s2.1`
- Output — what comes out of the stoma. You will hear it used far more often than you might expect `3.s2.2`
- Mucocutaneous junction — where the stoma meets your skin `3.s2.3`

**Your people** `3.s3`

- NSWOC — Nurse Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence. The Canadian specialist for stoma care, and the term used nationally `3.s3.1`
- ET nurse or enterostomal therapy nurse — the older term for the same role. It still appears in official documents, including Saskatchewan’s SAIL program rules `3.s3.2`
- WOCN Society — the American organization, which you will meet in US-published material. There the nurse is a WOC nurse, and a certified one is a CWOCN `3.s3.3`

### 04 · One-Piece vs Two-Piece
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- One-piece: barrier and pouch are joined — simple and low-profile `4.1`
- Two-piece: barrier stays while you change pouches — flexible for frequent emptying `4.2`
- Your NSWOC or pharmacist can help you find what seals best for your body `4.3`

### 05 · Skin Comfort
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Clean with warm water; avoid oils, fragrances, and lotion under the barrier `5.1`
- Pat dry completely — dry skin seals better than damp skin `5.2`
- Powder, paste, rings, and wipes are tools for seal and comfort — add only what you need `5.3`

### 06 · Output & Patterns
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Empty drainable pouches at about one-third to one-half full `6.1`
- Closed pouches are replaced as needed through the day `6.2`
- Full system changes are often every few days — or sooner if you feel burning, itching, or a leak `6.3`

### 07 · Fit Changes
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Measure at every change for the first six to eight weeks after surgery, and again after a weight change — stoma size can change as swelling settles ✎ `7.1`
- An opening that is too large exposes skin; too small can injure the stoma `7.2`
- Aim for a close fit around the stoma edge so output lands in the pouch, not on skin `7.3`

### 08 · When to Ask
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Persistent leaks, redness, pain, or skin that will not heal `8.1`
- Sudden changes in output, swelling, or how your barrier wears `8.2`
- Your NSWOC is the clinical guide; Ontario pharmacists can help with everyday product questions in chat `8.3`

### 09 · Measure before you order
Group: **The basics** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Use the measuring guide that comes in the box — hold it over the stoma and pick the closest shape and size `9.1`
- Cut so the opening sits close to the edge of the stoma. Too large exposes skin to output; too small can rub or injure the stoma `9.2`
- Not all stomas are round. Many are oval, and a cut-to-fit barrier can be shaped to match `9.3`

> **Note** `9.note` — Re-measure at every change for the first six to eight weeks after surgery, and again after any weight change or a hernia. A barrier cut to a size from before your last weight change is one of the most common reasons a system that used to work suddenly does not. ✎

### 10 · One-piece or two-piece
Group: **Choosing a system** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What tends to suit a one-piece** `10.s1`

- You want the lowest profile under clothes, and the simplest routine `10.s1.1`
- Your skin is settled and you are not changing the pouch more often than the barrier `10.s1.2`

**What tends to suit a two-piece** `10.s2`

- You empty or swap pouches often and would rather not disturb the barrier each time `10.s2.1`
- You want to alternate between a closed pouch for going out and a drainable one at home `10.s2.2`
- Reaching or dexterity is difficult, and doing the two steps separately is easier `10.s2.3`

> **Note** `10.s2.note` — Neither is better. Plenty of people use both — a two-piece for workdays and a one-piece for swimming, for instance.

### 11 · Flat or convex — please ask before you switch
Group: **Choosing a system** · Referral chip: **Needs an assessment first** *(warning tone — do not act on this page alone)* · Products shown: *none*

- A flat barrier suits a stoma that protrudes onto reasonably even skin, which is most people `11.1`
- Convexity curves toward your skin to help a flat or retracted stoma stand out, or to smooth a dip or crease that output keeps tracking into `11.2`
- It comes in soft and firm versions and different depths, and the right one depends on your abdomen, your stoma, and how your skin behaves under pressure `11.3`

> **Note** `11.note` — This is the one product decision on the whole site that we would rather you did not make alone. Convexity applied to the wrong abdomen can cause a pressure injury, and it is a common reason people end up with skin damage they did not have before. Ask your NSWOC to assess you — most will let you try one before you buy a box.

### 12 · What accessories actually do
Group: **Accessories** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**For sealing and skin** `12.s1`

- Barrier rings and seals — mouldable, they fill small dips and add a little protection right at the stoma edge `12.s1.1`
- Paste — not glue. It is a filler for creases and uneven skin. Most contain alcohol, so it can sting on broken skin `12.s1.2`
- Stoma powder — for weepy, broken skin only, dusted on and the excess brushed off. It does not belong under an intact barrier on healthy skin `12.s1.3`
- Barrier film or wipes — a thin protective layer between adhesive and skin, useful if removal is irritating your skin `12.s1.4`

**For comfort and confidence** `12.s2`

- Adhesive remover — reduces the pulling on your skin at removal, which matters more the more often you change `12.s2.1`
- Belts — add security and are sometimes recommended alongside convexity. They need sizing `12.s2.2`
- Lubricating deodorant — helps output drop to the bottom of the pouch and controls odour, which also helps with pancaking `12.s2.3`

> **Note** `12.s2.note` — What none of them do is rescue a barrier that is the wrong size or the wrong shape for you. If you are reaching for two or three accessories to make one system stay on, the system is the problem — that is a fit review, not a shopping list.

### 13 · Try it before you buy a box
Group: **Accessories** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Hollister, Coloplast and Convatec all send free samples in Canada, whether or not you buy from them, and regardless of which brand you currently use `13.1`
- Ask for a sample of anything you are considering switching to — barriers, rings, convex products, belts `13.2`
- Give a new product a few changes before deciding. First impressions are often about unfamiliarity rather than fit `13.3`

> **Note** `13.note` — Their contact details are in Everyday Liivving. There is no obligation attached, and it is a much cheaper way to find what works than buying full boxes.

### 14 · When to ask for a fit review
Group: **Keep checking** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Leaks that have started happening when they were not before `14.1`
- Weight change in either direction, which alters the shape of the area around your stoma `14.2`
- A new bulge, or the skin around the stoma changing shape `14.3`
- Skin that is not fully healed by the next change `14.4`
- Pregnancy, or any further abdominal surgery `14.5`

> **Note** `14.note` — A fit review is a normal part of ostomy care, not an admission that something has gone wrong. Bodies change, and the system that suited you last year may simply not be the right one now.

### 15 · Leaks and short wear time
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What often helps** `15.s1`

- Re-measure. Stoma size changes over the first six to eight weeks after surgery, and again after a weight change — an opening cut to last month’s size is one of the most common causes of a leak ✎ `15.s1.1`
- Check where the leak starts — from under the barrier, or from the edge. They point at different problems `15.s1.2`
- Make sure skin is completely dry before the barrier goes on, and hold it in place so body heat can set the seal `15.s1.3`

**When to call your NSWOC** `15.s2`

- Leaks more than occasionally, or a pattern you cannot explain `15.s2.1`
- Skin that has not fully healed between changes `15.s2.2`

> **Note** `15.s2.note` — Repeated leaking usually means the fit is wrong, not that you are doing it wrong. Convexity, rings and pastes can all help — but which one depends on your abdomen and your stoma, so that is an assessment rather than a shopping decision. The wrong convexity can cause a pressure injury.

### 16 · Pancaking
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What is happening** `16.s1`

- The pouch film sticks to itself, so output cannot drop away from the stoma and pushes up under the barrier instead `16.s1.1`
- It is more common with thicker output and with filters that pull the air out quickly `16.s1.2`

**What often helps** `16.s2`

- A puff of air in the pouch before you close it `16.s2.1`
- A lubricating deodorant, which helps output slide to the bottom `16.s2.2`

> **Note** `16.s2.note` — If it is constant, or your output has become noticeably thicker than it used to be, mention it — that is worth looking at rather than working around.

### 17 · Ballooning and gas
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What often helps** `17.s1`

- Filters do wet out and stop working — that is normal rather than a fault `17.s1.1`
- Gas patterns often settle over the first months as your gut adjusts `17.s1.2`
- Eating and drinking more slowly means swallowing less air `17.s1.3`

**When to call your NSWOC** `17.s2`

- A sudden change in gas alongside pain, or output that stops `17.s2.1`

> **Note** `17.s2.note` — Food affects gas differently for everyone, and post-surgery advice differs by ostomy type — so this is a conversation with your team or a dietitian rather than a list to follow.

### 18 · Sore, itchy, or weeping skin
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**Please do not self-diagnose this one** `18.s1`

- Irritation from output, a fungal rash, a contact allergy, and a few less common conditions look almost identical to the eye `18.s1.1`
- They have opposite treatments — the wrong one makes several of them worse `18.s1.2`

**What is safe to do meanwhile** `18.s2`

- Keep the area clean with warm water only — no oils, lotions, or fragranced products under the barrier `18.s2.1`
- Check the opening is not cut larger than the stoma, which leaves skin exposed to output `18.s2.2`
- Photograph it before your appointment, since skin changes between changes `18.s2.3`

> **Note** `18.s2.note` — Any skin that is broken, weeping, bleeding, or still not healed by the next change needs an NSWOC to look at it — not a product recommendation from the internet.

### 19 · Output that changes
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

**Why it matters more with an ileostomy** `19.s1`

- An ileostomy puts out more fluid and more salt, so dehydration builds faster and less obviously than people expect `19.s1.1`
- Thirst is not a reliable early sign — dark urine, headache, and feeling washed out often come first `19.s1.2`

**When to call** `19.s2`

- A sustained jump in output lasting more than a day `19.s2.1`
- Watery, high-volume output that is not settling `19.s2.2`
- Feeling dizzy, confused, or unusually weak alongside it `19.s2.3`

> **Note** `19.s2.note` — High output is the leading reason people are readmitted after ostomy surgery. It is worth phoning about early rather than waiting to see.

### 20 · A bulge around the stoma
Group: **When something is not right** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

**What it usually is** `20.s1`

- A parastomal hernia — the abdominal wall weakening around the stoma. It is common and it is not something you caused `20.s1.1`
- It often changes how your barrier sits, so leaks can start at the same time `20.s1.2`

**When to call your NSWOC** `20.s2`

- Any new bulge, or a change in the shape of the area around your stoma `20.s2.1`

> **Note** `20.s2.note` — Support garments help many people, but they have to be sized and chosen for the specific hernia — buying one without an assessment can make the fit worse rather than better.

### 21 · Clothing & Confidence
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

- High-waisted styles and soft layers can keep a pouch secure and low-profile `21.1`
- Support belts or wraps for active days when you want extra hold `21.2`
- You do not have to hide your pouch — comfort and preference come first `21.3`

### 22 · Travel & Workdays
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- Empty when the pouch is about one-third to one-half full to reduce leak risk `22.1`
- Pack supplies in your carry-on — never only in checked bags `22.2`
- Plan bathroom stops the way you plan coffee: early and without apology `22.3`

### 23 · Intimacy & Social Ease
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

- Talk about what helps you feel secure — timing, clothing, or a support wrap `23.1`
- Confidence grows with a routine that has already worked at home `23.2`
- Your pace is the right pace `23.3`

### 24 · Rest & Routine
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- Many people prefer morning changes when output is often lower `24.1`
- Lay out supplies like a station before you start `24.2`
- Restock before you run low — clockwork beats last-minute stress `24.3`

### 25 · Hernias, lifting and your core
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- A parastomal hernia is a bulge beside the stoma, where the abdominal wall has weakened and what is underneath pushes through. It is common, and more likely the longer you have a stoma. Ordinary daily life does not cause it, though not smoking, keeping to a healthy weight and avoiding straining all lower the risk `25.1`
- Follow the lifting advice your surgical team gives you, and ask them to show you how to lift rather than only what to avoid. Your abdominal wall is still healing in the early weeks, so build up gradually — technique matters more than a fixed weight limit `25.2`
- Gentle core and breathing exercises usually start within the first few days, and you build from there. What is right for you depends on your fitness as much as your surgery — a physiotherapist can set the pace with you `25.3`

> **Note** `25.note` — Many people find a support garment comfortable and reassuring, particularly if a hernia is already there. It is worth knowing that support wear has not been shown to prevent a hernia — it is for comfort and confidence. If you have one, ask your NSWOC to measure and fit you, since a garment that is too tight can restrict your movement and breathing.

### 26 · Getting back to activity
Group: **Body and life** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

- Walking usually comes first and starts early. Everything beyond that is a conversation about timing with your surgical team `26.1`
- Swimming is fine once your wounds are fully healed — your pouch is water-resistant and, fitted well, designed not to leak. Change it well before you swim rather than just beforehand so the adhesive can settle, and cover the filter with the sticker provided `26.2`
- Contact sports are worth raising, since a stoma guard protects against a direct blow. Heavy lifting is a separate question — a guard does not help there. Technique, breathing out on the effort and building up gradually do, and most people get back to what they did before `26.3`

> **Note** `26.note` — Ostomy Canada and the manufacturer support programs both run activity resources, and plenty of ostomates return to running, swimming, weights, and team sport.

## Emergency red flags

**Some things are not a website question** `urgent.heading`

Most stoma worries can wait for your next NSWOC appointment. These cannot. Seek urgent medical care if you notice: `urgent.intro`

1. A stoma that turns dark, dusky, purple, or feels cold to the touch `urgent.1`
2. Severe abdominal pain, or vomiting with no output for several hours — this can mean a blockage `urgent.2`
3. Heavy or continuous bleeding from the stoma itself, not just a spot from cleaning `urgent.3`
4. Fever, or skin around the stoma that is hot, spreading red, and painful `urgent.4`
5. Confusion, severe dizziness, or very dark urine alongside high output — signs of significant dehydration `urgent.5`
6. A Mitrofanoff you cannot pass a catheter through — an unemptied bladder will not wait. A bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch is different: see “The less common diversions” in Chapter 02 for what to try first ✎ `urgent.6`

**Action** `urgent.action` — Go to your nearest emergency department or call 911. Do not wait for a callback, and do not troubleshoot a dusky stoma at home.

## Pharmacist panel

- **eyebrow** `pharmacist.eyebrow` — Available in Ontario
- **heading** `pharmacist.heading` — Ask without the awkward
- **body** `pharmacist.body` — Not sure if you need convex, a ring, or a different wipe? Chat with an Ontario pharmacist during business hours — until 5 p.m. Eastern. For clinical stoma concerns, your NSWOC remains your primary resource.
- **cta** `pharmacist.cta` — Talk to a Pharmacist

## Closing

**Comfort is a skill you build** `closing.heading`

Knowing your stoma is not a test — it is a quieter relationship with fit, skin, and the products that earn their place on your shelf. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for assessment by your NSWOC, surgeon, or physician. Fit, skin, and product choices depend on your body and your surgery — talk to your care team before changing anything. `disclaimer`

## Corrections waiting on re-review

*Marked ✎ above. These lines were corrected in the source and are live now; they need the RN and the NSWOC to read them again and either keep or reword them. No figure or link is held on this — the wording is what is in question.*

- `15.s1.1` — Was: “Re-measure. Stoma size changes for months after surgery, and an opening cut to last month’s size is one of the most common causes of a leak” — Same correction, and the weight change is now named here too, because this line is the one a reader reaches while chasing a leak.
- `7.1` — Was: “Measure during the first months — stoma size can change as swelling settles” — Canadian sources put a period on it: measure at every change while the stoma shrinks over the first six to eight weeks after surgery, then again after a weight change (NSWOCC ileostomy guide; Kingston Health Sciences ileostomy booklet; CLWK one-piece procedure). "The first months" also contradicted Chapter 01 step 7, which the same sources wrote. The weight change is named here as well, so this line, 9.note, 15.s1.1 and the figure line on card 9 all say the same thing. Please also settle whether re-measuring should be said to STOP at eight weeks: the NSWOCC colostomy guide says "measure at each full change" with no end date, and card 14 lists weight change, a new bulge, pregnancy and further surgery as ongoing reasons to have the fit looked at.
- `9.note` — Was: “Re-measure regularly for the first few months, and again after any weight change or a hernia. A barrier cut to a size from two months ago is one of the most common reasons a system that used to work suddenly does not.” — Same correction, on the card Chapter 01's walk-through links to for the gap. The second sentence changed with it: it used to name "a size from two months ago" as the common failure, which is eight to nine weeks — the point at which the corrected first sentence stops asking for routine re-measuring, so the two sentences called the same cut both correct and a common fault. It now names the thing that actually changes the size, "a size from before your last weight change". PLEASE READ BOTH SENTENCES TOGETHER. The weight change and the hernia are otherwise unchanged.
- `urgent.6` — Was: “A catheter that will not pass, if you empty a continent diversion or a Mitrofanoff that way — a reservoir that cannot be drained will not wait” — One presentation had two thresholds on one page. This line sat under "Go to your nearest emergency department or call 911" and said a reservoir that cannot be drained "will not wait", while card 2's note gives a bowel reservoir such as a Kock pouch a graded instruction — stop, rest an hour, try again, and get advice that day. The list now keeps only the case that is unambiguously an emergency, and points at the card for the rest instead of restating it differently. The NSWOC still has to set the threshold for each diversion type.
